Bay Mills Indian Community

Bay Mills Indian Community is a distinct Ojibwe government and community whose public history work connects photographs, documents, elder interviews and education. Its History Department describes a committee working with scholar Charles Cleland on The Place of the Pike, a history of Bay Mills, and explains Gnoozhekaaning as the local traditional place name. The department's account also connects constitutional organization in 1936 with the first tribal election in 1937. This is Bay Mills' institutional narrative, rather than a claim that every regional Ojibwe community shares the same government history. Bay Mills Community College provides another specific community institution: its account traces a vocational program funded in 1981 and a charter granted by Bay Mills Indian Community in 1984. The college describes serving the local community, other tribal communities and neighbors through several locations and online education. These sources make a useful first path through community memory and institution building. Present program access, educational outcomes and detailed historical chronology remain questions for further review.

01

History assembled within the community

The History Department describes collecting photographs and documents and interviewing elders in work that supported Charles Cleland's book. Its public account is a guide to that community effort, not a substitute for reading the book or assessing every underlying archive. Sensitive burial entries are omitted from this profile.

Read the sources [1] Bay Mills Indian Community

02

A tribally chartered college

The college traces its origins to a vocational program and its 1984 charter from Bay Mills Indian Community. Its own institutional account places education alongside regional community development. The pictured college is a particular community institution; it does not represent all Bay Mills people or establish current course availability.
